messages.subject: [statnet_help] Significant memory use for gof.ergmm
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm trying to use the gof.ergmm function from the latentnet package, and it
seems to be creating unexpectedly large gofobject objects, which is causing
problems when I'm trying to save a goodness of fit object from several
networks.  Does anyone know why, or how to fix it?  I've included more
detail, and a possible partial solution below.

Here's an example:

> rm(list = ls())> library(statnet)> > # Library for memory use; see http://adv-r.had.co.nz/memory.html> library(pryr)> > data(sampson)> samp.fit <- ergmm(samplike ~ euclidean(d = 2))> > samp.gof <- gof(samp.fit)> object_size(samp.gof)6.98 MB

Running gof.ergmm on the example from the documentation gives a 7MB file.
For a single network, this isn't a huge problem -- my computer isn't
choking on 7MB -- but it becomes a problem when you try to loop over many
model fits, for many networks.

My best guess is that R is doing a poor job of garbage collection at the
end of the gof.ergmm function.  The gof.ergmm function simulates several
networks from the model fit, and then calculates statistics using those.
When it's done, it doesn't seem to return the memory used by the
simulations.  Adding a rm(SimNetworkSeriesObj) statement in the function
seems to produce much smaller gofobject objects, presumably because then R
returns the memory used by the simulations.  Code for this is below
(apologies for the length -- I copied and pasted the gof.ergmm function).

messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet Users,

Do you run statnet on windows- or mac-based MPI parallel computing
clusters?  Are you aware of any statnet users or colleagues who use a
non-unix cluster? If so, please let me know.

The statnet team is in the process of overhauling and improving the 
parallelization functionality in ergm, and we are trying to determine if 
non-unix clusters are something we need to actively support for statnet 
-- which would require that we devote additional time to testing and 
maintaining the functionality on other platforms.

If we do de-prioritize testing on non-unix MPI clusters, we would of 
course still support single machine multicore parallel functionality on 
all three platforms.

best,
  -skye

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

If I understand it correctly, then we might get biased estimates on the
homophily parameters (the nodematch term) if some groups are just much more
"sociable" than others, and therefore I should also always add a nodefactor
term, correct?

However, what if I suspect that the network of interest is determined not
simply by belonging to one or another group, but by the underlying social
structure within the groups and therefore instead include an edgecov term
(and enter the network that represents this underlying social structure, in
my case a complex star network with quite a few isolates).

Is there an equivalent to the nodefactor term that I should add to avoid
bias (e.g. a nodefactor term for "part of underlying network vs. isolate")?

Thanks in advance for any suggestions,

Franziska


--

Franziska Barbara Keller
PhD Candidate, Department of Politics, New York University

Hi,

I ran into a possible bug with network.arrow(). Basically, when you specify
the "curve" option, the arrows look strange. I have documented this
phenomenon on stackoverflow at:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/25777757/r-network-arrow-looks-strange-when-curved

Alternately, you can simply run the following code to generate an example:

library(maps)
library(network)
map("usa")
network.arrow(-110,37,-85,40,length=5,width=1,angle=20,curve=2)

To whom it may concern, I am running Mac OSX 10.9.5 with R version 3.02. My
network package is version 1.10.2.

Sincerely,

Warren Ronsiek

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 4-cycles
messages.body_plain:
Just to comment further on this, the dyadwise shared partner (DSP) terms 
of order >=2 will measure the concentration of 4-cycles on arbitrary 
dyads; if you want 4-cycles _with at most one chord_, then the nullwise 
shared partners  (NSPs) of order >=2 will pick this up.  (ESPs >=2 will 
correspondingly capture 4-cycles with at _least_ one chord.) As Martina 
noted, none of these are directly counting the 4-cycles per se, so one 
would need to be careful in their interpretation vis a vis 
cycle-specific mechanisms.  Also, gwdsp/gwnsp/gwesp will put weight on 
DSP/NSP/ESP terms of order 0 and 1 (which do not contain 4-cycles), so 
this may require correction.

While it is true that the k-cycles for k>3 are not provably safe 
statistics, in my experience they are often better behaved than the 
triangle term.  "Often" does not mean "always."  They can certainly 
produce poor results...on the other hand, I'm currently fitting models 
with cycle lengths as large as 10 to networks with >250 nodes.  Much 
depends on the details of the network, the other terms in the model, 
constraints, etc.

One additional point that bears note is that a 4-cycle term with a 
negative parameter (as proposed here) will not lead e.g. to the density 
explosion route to degeneracy.  That does not in and of itself guarantee 
good behavior, but as a practical matter it is usually the positive 
terms that cause problems.  (An easy way to probe the impact of such a 
term is to refit the model with the cycle term as an offset, and examine 
the behavior of simulated networks under the refitted model as a 
function of the offset parameter.  This can be useful in identifying 
whether e.g. models in the portion of the parameter space that is of 
interest are well-behaved, one is close to a phase transition, etc.)

Cycles are a rich source of interesting problems, of both the good kind 
and the bad kind.  Hopefully, the above observations will prove useful 
to those seeking to employ cycle terms in their models!

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hello Narges,

I just took a look at your degree distributions to make sure that they 
were in balance (female total degree = male total degree) and indeed 
they are, so that's good.

Looking at the actual distributions, my suspicion is that the issue is 
just with the females (of whom very few are above degree 1; 20 with 
degree 2 and 3 with degree 3) but not with the men (where the 
corresponding figures are 136 and 36).  You tried reducing the terms for 
both females and males, and that prevented the eror but provided poor 
fit.  I would try just reducing the females down to a single degree 
term, but leaving the males at both.

Also, I notice that you don't have a maximum degree constraint in the 
model.  Did you intend to?  If so, the argument would be 
constraints=~bd(maxout=3).  That might add to your problems with 
computational singularity, or it might actually be the trick you need.  
Perhaps that in combination with one of the reduced models will be the 
combo you need.

Yours,
Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris and Nate,

I think there are two important things here: modeling the distribution 
of the relation(s) adequately, and deciding whether it's necessary and 
useful to model them jointly in one dependent variable. The alternative 
would be to model them separately and include each relation or a 
transformation thereof as a covariate (which would make it easier to 
think of endogenous network statistics), but I assume you have already 
tried that. Given that you are quite sure that both should be modeled 
jointly, you could accommodate both relations/networks in a single 
matrix (with each node being duplicated, e.g., in a block-diagonal 
matrix) and set the type of nodes (i.e., which original network relation 
is this node from?) as a nodal covariate. Then you would have to come up 
with statistics that describe the features of the joint network, for 
example a statistic counting how often x_ij from relation 1 and x_ij 
from relation 2 are both tied (= cross-relation reciprocity), or how 
often x_ij and x_jk form a two-path in relation 1 AND x_ik are tied in 
relation 2 or vice-versa (= cross-relation triadic closure), and so on. 
This is kind of the bottleneck because you would presumably have to 
implement some of these statistics on your own while others can probably 
be implemented using covariates (as suggested by Nate in his example). 
For example, if you want to model interdependent triadic closure as in a 
collaboration and conflict setting (where A and C are likely to have a 
positive tie when A and B as well as B and C have negative ties, due to 
social balance), you can most likely do that by creating a covariate 
matrix which contains the two-paths of relation 1 as direct ties in the 
block of relation 2 and possibly vice-versa. That might work, but I am 
still a bit hesitant because simple triadic closure and other simpler 
network statistics might actually look very different across the two 
relations, and modeling these different distributions through one joint 
model term at a time may not necessarily capture their joint 
distribution very well. It may also be problematic because things like 
social balance may not necessarily work in the same way for both 
relations or directions (--+ is social balance, but ++- would not be 
balanced), so you really have to think about theory and about how to 
accommodate this in covariate matrices. So I would say it's possible in 
principle but use it cautiously.

Funny coincidence: the two of you are located at Columbus and Amherst, 
and I am currently a visiting scholar at OSU in Columbus and will then 
move on to Amherst for a couple of days in mid-November.

I hope that's helpful.

Best,
Philip

On 10/26/2014 11:41 AM, Fischer, Jason Donald wrote:
> I have a question about the interpretation of nodemix coefficients. 
> Let's say I have a simple model looking at associations among sexes 
> and I use the default of 0 for the base option [edges +nodemix("sex")] .
>
> If the coefficient for male-male associations was significant and 
> positive, would it be correct to interpret this as
> male-male associations positively affect (i.e., increase) the 
> likelihood of edges occurring in the network? Would it also be 
> accurate to say that male-male associations are more likely to occur 
> than expected by chance given the density of the network?
>
> If a base was specified (say it was set to female-female associations) 
> and the male-male coefficient was still significant and positive, 
> would the interpretation change to edges are more likely occur between 
> males than between females? Or does the base option just specify terms 
> that are not of interest and should be left out of the model?
Hi Jason,

I think it'll be most clear if I walk through three models in turn. Let 
me create a network with a single attribute, and then purely random ties 
unrelated to that attribute. Because this is undirected, there are only 
a total of three kinds of attribute combos, not four:

 > library(ergm)
 > aaa <- network.initialize(100, directed=F)
 > aaa %v% 'sex' <- sample(c('F','M'),100, replace=T)
 > aaa <- simulate(ergm(aaa~edges,target.stats=200))

First, if you have a nodemix term with a base of 0 and you *don't* have 
an edges term, then you can interpret each coefficient in there as an 
effect for that type of tie.  But note that you are *not* conditioning 
on the density of the network in this case, because there is no edges 
term.  If nodemix were the only term in your model, then the 
coefficients would all be defined as the propensity for that type of 
tie, relative to a density of 0.5.  Note how the coefficients are all 
roughly equal to each other; each is defined relative to a density of 0.5:

 > (ccc <- ergm(aaa~nodemix('sex')))

MLE Coefficients:
mix.sex.F.F  mix.sex.F.M  mix.sex.M.M
      -3.185       -3.211       -3.104

Second, if you have an edges and nodemix term, and you leave one 
category out as a base, then the edges term can be interpreted in terms 
of the propensity for ties of the omitted category, and the others can 
be interpreted as the propensity for the various groups, relative to the 
omitted category:

 > (ddd <- ergm(aaa~edges+nodemix('sex',base=1)))

MLE Coefficients:
       edges  mix.sex.F.M  mix.sex.M.M
    -3.18475     -0.02635      0.08064

Note how here the edges coefficient is equal to the nodemix.FF 
coefficient in the previous model; and the other two represent the 
difference between that value and the other values in the previous model.

Finally, if you have a nodemix with a base of 0 in combination with an 
edges term, then you will end up with collinearity: one of your terms 
will be dropped out.  E.g.:

 > (bbb <- ergm(aaa~edges+nodemix('sex')))

MLE Coefficients:
       edges  mix.sex.F.F  mix.sex.F.M  mix.sex.M.M
    -3.10411     -0.08064     -0.10699           NA

HTH,
Steve
